meta.description: R. Buckminster Fuller, in his poem 'No More Secondhand God', written 9 April 1940 and published in 1963. It is verse, not prose — and the commas have moved.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'God, to me, it seems is a verb, not a noun, proper or improper'?
meta.ogDescription: Buckminster Fuller wrote it as verse on 9 April 1940. Published 1963 in 'No More Secondhand God'. The popular version moves a comma.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1895–1983 · American architect, systems theorist, inventor and futurist
answer.sourceLine: From Fuller’s long poem No More Secondhand God, which dates itself in its opening lines — ‘Late tonight (April 9, 1940)’ — and was published as the title piece of a 1963 collection ↗. Two things to know: it is verse, printed in short broken lines, and the circulating prose version moves a comma. Fuller’s page reads ‘for God, to me, it seems, / is a verb / not a noun, / proper or improper;’

source.heading: A poem that dates itself

source.excerpt:
Here is God's purpose—
for God, to me, it seems,
is a verb
not a noun,
proper or improper;
is the articulation
not the art, objective or subjective;
is loving,
not the abstraction "love" commanded or entreated;
is knowledge dynamic,
not legislative code,
not proclamation law,
not academic dogma, nor ecclesiastic canon.

Yes, God is a verb,
the most active,
connoting the vast harmonic
reordering of the universe
from unleashed chaos of energy.
trail: The passage is on p. 22 of No More Secondhand God and Other Writings, scanned in full at the Internet Archive ↗. The book’s copyright page reads ‘Copyright (c) 1963 by R. Buckminster Fuller’ and notes it ‘was originally published by Southern Illinois University Press, in 1963’.

The date comes from the poem and from Fuller himself, not from a secondary source. The poem opens ‘Late tonight / (April 9, 1940)’, and in the book’s preface Fuller writes: ‘The poem “No More Secondhand God” was written in 1940 as I sought to discipline my mind into the development of tools of communication which might render democracy more effective in the era of the increasing political dictatorships.’

Wikiquote also cites the line to No More Secondhand God (1963) ↗ and, like us, sets it as verse — though its transcription places the comma after ‘verb’ rather than after ‘seems’, where the printed page has it.
source.cutTag: No More Secondhand God and Other Writings (1963), p. 22
source.excerptNote: The line breaks are Fuller’s. Note also that the famous four-word condensation — ‘God is a verb’ — is genuinely his too: it appears again a few lines later, as ‘Yes, God is a verb, the most active…’

author.bio: Richard Buckminster Fuller Jr. (1895–1983), who signed himself R. Buckminster Fuller, was an American architect, systems theorist, inventor and futurist, and the author of more than thirty books. He coined or popularised Spaceship Earth, Dymaxion, ephemeralization, synergetics and tensegrity. He wrote a good deal of his philosophy as verse, and in 1970 published a book titled I Seem to Be a Verb.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost in the retelling
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right. What the circulating version loses is the punctuation, the line breaks, and the fact that this is a poem about democracy.

items.why: The printed page reads ‘for God, to me, it seems, / is a verb / not a noun, / proper or improper;’ — comma after seems, none after verb. The popular prose form drops the first and adds the second, which quietly turns Fuller’s hesitant aside into a flat declaration.

It is verse. Fuller set it in short broken lines, and the jacket copy of his own book calls these pieces ‘prose-poem essays’ and quotes his description of them as ‘mental mouthfuls and ventilated prose’. Flattening it into a sentence is how it ends up read as theology rather than as poetry.

Only in part. By Fuller’s own account in the preface, No More Secondhand God was written to propose ‘practical means for daily or hourly telephone voting by democracy’ in ‘the era of the increasing political dictatorships’ — an idea he later said evolved into his notion of two-way beamed television.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Fuller’s, written on 9 April 1940 and printed on p. 22 of his 1963 collection ↗ — as five lines of verse, not one sentence.

context.heading: God as process, not thing
lead: Fuller’s objection is grammatical before it is theological. A noun is a thing you can own, name and argue about; a verb is something that happens. So he lists what God is not — not ‘the abstraction “love” commanded or entreated’, not ‘legislative code’, not ‘proclamation law’, not ‘academic dogma, nor ecclesiastic canon’ — and what it is instead: ‘the articulation, not the art’, ‘loving’, ‘knowledge dynamic’.
detailsBody: ‘No more secondhand God’ is the point: Fuller is against receiving the universe on someone else’s authority. Earlier in the same poem he says the instruments do the talking — the two-hundred-inch telescope, the electron microscope, ‘the actual achievement of atomic energy, released and controllable’ — and that ‘only now, through the impersonal “word” of these scientific instruments, does God speak of them to our widening comprehension’. The telephone-voting proposal is the same instinct applied to politics: stop being told, and measure directly.
He kept returning to the grammar. In 1970 he published a whole book under the title I Seem to Be a Verb — the same argument, turned on himself.

sourcesVerified.claim: On p. 22 the book prints, as verse: "Here is God's purpose-- / for God, to me, it seems, / is a verb / not a noun, / proper or improper; / is the articulation / not the art..." and fifteen lines later "Yes, God is a verb, / the most active...". The poem opens "Late tonight / (April 9, 1940)". The copyright page reads "Copyright (c) 1963 by R. Buckminster Fuller" and "This book was originally published by Southern Illinois University Press, in 1963", with "Anchor Books Edition: 1971". Fuller's preface states the poem "was written in 1940... ‘No More Secondhand God’ proposes practical means for daily or hourly telephone voting by democracy".
Wikiquote attributes the line to No More Secondhand God (1963), rendering it as verse with the comma after 'verb' rather than after 'seems'.
Richard Buckminster Fuller Jr. lived July 12, 1895 - July 1, 1983, styled his name R. Buckminster Fuller, and published more than 30 books.
